reason: This passage (Exodus 32, the Golden Calf narrative) portrays the Hebrew leaders as executing religious law and enforcing covenant observance rather than being antagonistic to their people. Aaron, confronted by the people's demand, accommodates rather than opposes them—he creates the calf, builds an altar, and proclaims a festival. Moses, upon discovering the apostasy, takes harsh punitive action (ordering the execution of approximately 3,000 idolaters), but this is framed within a religious discipline framework—enforcement of God's law against those who violated their covenant commitments. Earlier in the text, Moses even intercedes on behalf of the people with God, arguing against their complete destruction. The leaders' actions are presented as correction and law enforcement, not as antagonism rooted in opposition to the people themselves.
